## Warm-Up: Quick Concept and Calculation Checks

a. To fight a recession, should the Fed use *expansionary* or *contractionary* monetary policy?
   What happens to interest rates under that policy?
b. Name the Fed's key policymaking committee that sets the federal funds rate target.
c. If the Fed wants to *lower* interest rates through open market operations, does it buy or sell
   government bonds? (Recall bond prices and interest rates from Chapter 14.)
d. What is *forward guidance*, and how can it affect the economy even before the Fed changes any
   rate?
e. When are quantitative easing (QE) and quantitative tightening (QT) typically used, compared to
   ordinary open market operations?
f. True or False: monetary policy is equally effective at fighting inflation and at pulling an
   economy out of a severe recession.
g. Why does the Fed target roughly 2 percent inflation rather than 0 percent?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. *Expansionary.* Interest rates *fall*.
b. The *Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)*.
c. It *buys* bonds. Buying bonds bids up bond prices, and since bond prices and interest rates move
   inversely, this pushes interest rates down.
d. Forward guidance is the Fed communicating its outlook and future policy intentions. If the Fed
   is credible, businesses and investors adjust their spending and investment plans immediately
   based on what the Fed says it intends to do, even before any rate actually changes.
e. QE and QT are typically used when short-term rates are already very low (near the zero lower
   bound) and the Fed wants to influence *longer-term* rates directly, ordinary open market
   operations mainly target short-term rates.
f. *False.* Monetary policy is relatively reliable at slowing an overheating economy, but less
   reliable at pulling an economy out of a severe recession (cyclical asymmetry and the liquidity
   trap).
g. A little inflation lets *real* wages adjust downward even when nominal wages are sticky and
   rarely get cut outright, this helps labor markets adjust more smoothly than a 0 percent target
   would.

</details>

## Problem 1: Movement Along vs. a Shift in Investment Demand

For each event, determine whether it causes a *movement along* the investment demand curve or a
*shift* of the entire curve, and explain why.

a. The Fed actually cuts the federal funds rate target by half a percentage point this week.
b. The Fed chair gives a speech strongly signaling that rate cuts are likely in the coming months,
   with no rate change happening yet.
c. A new technology lowers the cost of building factories across the economy.
d. Long-term interest rates fall because the Fed begins a new round of quantitative easing.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. *Movement along* the curve. An actual change in the interest rate moves firms along their
   existing investment demand curve to a new quantity of investment.
b. *Shift* of the entire curve (to the right, more investment demanded at every interest rate). No
   rate has actually changed yet, businesses are adjusting their plans purely because of the
   credible signal about the future.
c. *Shift* of the entire curve (to the right). Lower costs make more projects profitable at every
   interest rate, this is a change in a non-interest determinant of investment.
d. *Movement along* the curve. Even though QE is an unusual tool, it works by actually changing the
   interest rate (here, a longer-term rate), so it still produces a movement along the existing
   investment demand curve, not a shift of it.

</details>

## Problem 2: Tracing the Monetary Policy Transmission Chain

The Fed cuts its target interest rate. As a result, businesses find an additional $30 billion in
investment projects newly profitable at the lower rate. The economy's MPC is 0.75.

a. What chapter's tool explains why a lower interest rate increases the quantity of investment
   demanded?
b. What is the multiplier?
c. Using the multiplier, by how much does this initial $30 billion increase in investment
   ultimately shift AD (in real GDP terms)?
d. In the AD-AS model, what happens to the equilibrium price level and equilibrium real GDP as a
   result of this AD shift, assuming the economy is not already at potential GDP?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["Initial rise in<br>investment", "Total shift in AD<br>(after multiplier)"],
                     y=[30, 120], marker_color=[BLUE, ORANGE],
                     text=["$30B", "$120B"], textposition="outside",
                     hovertemplate="%{x}: %{text}<extra></extra>"))
fig.update_layout(yaxis_title="Billions of dollars", width=520, height=400,
                  plot_bgcolor="white", showlegend=False)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", range=[0, 140])
fig.show()
```

a. The *investment demand curve* (Chapter 10): a lower real interest rate makes more investment
   projects profitable, increasing the quantity of investment demanded.
b. Multiplier $= 1/(1-0.75) = 4$.
c. $\Delta AD = 30 \times 4 = \$120$ billion.
d. Since AD shifts right along the upward-sloping SRAS curve (Chapter 12), the equilibrium *price
   level rises* and equilibrium *real GDP rises*, this is exactly the chain: Fed action to
   Chapter 10's investment demand to Chapter 10/11's multiplier to Chapter 12's AD-AS equilibrium.

</details>

## Problem 3: Cyclical Asymmetry and the Liquidity Trap

a. During a period of strong demand-pull inflation, the Fed raises interest rates sharply, and
   borrowing and spending slow noticeably within a few months. Does this illustrate the Fed's tools
   working *reliably* or *unreliably*?
b. During a severe recession, the Fed cuts its target rate all the way to nearly zero, but
   businesses remain too uncertain about the future to borrow, and banks remain too cautious to
   lend freely. What is this situation called?
c. In the situation from part (b), what other policy tool (from a previous chapter) might
   policymakers need to rely on instead?
d. Explain in one or two sentences why lower interest rates might fail to stimulate borrowing and
   lending during a severe downturn, even though the same tool works well to cool an overheating
   economy.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. *Reliably.* This illustrates the "slowing an expansion" side of cyclical asymmetry, where
   monetary policy tends to work well.
b. A *liquidity trap*.
c. *Fiscal policy* (Chapter 13), using government spending and taxes to directly boost aggregate
   demand when monetary policy alone cannot.
d. Lower rates only stimulate borrowing and lending if businesses are confident enough to invest and
   banks are confident enough to lend. During a severe downturn, uncertainty about the future can
   make both sides unwilling to act even at very low rates, breaking the normal chain from lower
   rates to more investment spending.

</details>
